John 3:16 is often heard and we believe it, but do we truly understand its power? It is the Gospel in a nutshell.
For God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in Him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
There is no more wonderful announcement in all the Word of God than what we read in this verse. Think of it, beloved! God is love.
To think that God could love a world that hated Him and demanded the death of His Son. He nailed Him to the cross and mocked Him while He died to redeem even those that hated Him.
That little word 'so' signifies that there are not enough words in all the languages of the world to explain the depth or the height of the great love God bestowed upon man.
The truth set forth in the Gospel is that God gave His Son to the world because He so loved the world that whosoever believeth in Him should not perish but have everlasting life.

Scientific forest management practices could nearly double the tree harvest from our 92 million acres of federally-owned commercial forests. It is frustrating to see nearly six billion board feet of softwood die and rot every year.

The pendulum has swung too far in one direction. Land is being set aside to lie fallow and unproductive. We need to intensify management on remaining lands to produce more timber per acre and make up for the loss.

As an American, you aren't getting your money's worth from our nation's treasure of forests. We need a national timber policy that plans for future supplies and the environment to the next century and beyond.

I just checked the latest hog prices and it's demoralizing. A year ago we were getting $60 per hundred; now it's dropped below $35. My production costs haven't dropped a cent, but my income just got cut nearly in half.
If the price of hogs has dropped 50% for the farmers, why am I still paying full price for pork chops at the grocery store? Somebody is making a lot of money in the middle while we all struggle.

It's important to remember that the 'farm dollar' only accounts for about 40 cents of the retail food price. The other 60 cents goes into processing, packaging, and shipping after the product leaves the farm gate.
We need to do a better job of connecting our urban neighbors with our local farms. Too many people think the supermarket is where food begins, rather than just the last stop on a very long journey.

The food production line is taking a heavy turn on the backs of family farmers. When farm prices go up, retail prices skyrocket, but when farm prices decline, retail prices seem to stay exactly where they are.

I remember when you could buy directly from your neighbor's farm without all these middlemen and 'detours'. The modern system is efficient, but we've lost that personal contact between the city and the farm.
